Male redear sunfish exhibit pronounced nest-guarding behavior during the spring spawning season, a period when water temperatures steadily rise. Females deposit their adhesive eggs over the nest substrate, and the newly hatched yolk-sac larvae rely entirely on their endogenous reserves during the first days of life. The wet weight at birth is approximately 0.0016 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0016 grams], a value consistent with the egg diameter of 1.45 millimeters typically observed for this species. This modest initial mass requires the prolarvae to efficiently absorb their yolk before transitioning to exogenous feeding on zooplankton. Following the resorption of the yolk sac, the free-swimming larvae disperse into the littoral zone, where they encounter abundant microcrustaceans. Growth during this pelagic larval phase is rapid under favorable thermal conditions, and individuals can attain a total length of approximately 15 centimeters by the end of their first year, which corresponds to the size at which sexual maturation begins. Thus, the total length at puberty is 15 centimeters [Lp = 15 centimeters], a measurement that aligns well with field observations of gonadal development in young-of-year fish collected from productive southeastern reservoirs.

As the fish continue their development into the sub-adult stage, the relationship between length and mass follows a predictable allometric trajectory. Using a length-weight equation derived from extensive sampling of this species, the body mass at the onset of puberty corresponds to a wet weight at puberty of approximately 56 grams [Wwp = approximately 56 grams]. This value marks a substantial increase from the birth mass, reflecting the accumulation of somatic tissue during the first growing season. Continued growth over subsequent years allows individuals to approach their maximum recorded size, and the ultimate total length has been documented at 35.5 centimeters [Li = 35.5 centimeters] in long-term population surveys. The corresponding ultimate wet weight reaches 793 grams [Wwi = 793 grams] for the largest adults, a figure that demonstrates the considerable size range encompassed across the species' lifespan. These asymptotic values are typically attained by older, slow-growing individuals that have completed their primary investment in somatic growth and are allocating resources toward annual reproductive efforts.

Reproductive output in redear sunfish is strongly influenced by water temperature, with spawning activity concentrated during the late spring and early summer months. Under a controlled thermal regime of 21 °C [T = 21 °C], the maximum reproductive rate of the species has been determined through observations of captive broodstock. Females produce approximately 220 eggs per nest [N_R_i = approximately 220 eggs per nest], and they can complete about one spawning event per day [F_R_i = about one spawning event per day] during the peak of the breeding season when conditions remain optimal. This high frequency of spawning is facilitated by the warm, stable temperatures that accelerate vitellogenesis and oocyte maturation. The daily rate at which a female can generate offspring is therefore considerable, allowing a single individual to contribute thousands of eggs to the population over the course of a single spawning season. This reproductive strategy is characteristic of many centrarchid species that inhabit productive, warm-water environments where early larval survival is high.

The natural lifespan of redear sunfish has been documented through mark-recapture studies and otolith annulus analysis across multiple populations. Under the stable thermal conditions typical of productive systems (21 °C [T = 21 °C]), the time since birth at death has been recorded at approximately 3285 days [am = approximately 3285 days] for the oldest known individuals. This longevity, equivalent to roughly nine years, places redear sunfish among the longer-lived members of the genus Lepomis. The extended lifespan is likely linked to their relatively slow growth at older ages and the reduced metabolic demands associated with a benthic, mollusk-dominated diet. Older individuals often exhibit thickened pharyngeal teeth, an adaptation for crushing snails, which constitutes a major component of their adult diet. This trophic specialization may reduce competition with other sunfishes and allow for stable energy intake throughout the year, contributing to the species' ability to achieve considerable ages in productive systems.

Comparative studies among centrarchids highlight the life-history strategy of redear sunfish as one characterized by moderate size at maturity, substantial reproductive investment, and notable longevity for a fish of its body plan. The interplay between size at first reproduction and maximum achievable length generates a life-history trajectory that balances early fecundity with continued somatic growth. The total length at which puberty initiates, 15 centimeters [Lp = 15 centimeters], represents approximately 42 percent of the ultimate total length of 35.5 centimeters [Li = 35.5 centimeters], a proportional relationship that is relatively conservative within the family. In addition, the wet weight of 0.0016 grams [Wwb = 0.0016 grams] at birth is typical for adhesive-egg spawners that provide parental care, while the shift to a wet weight at maturity of 56 grams [Wwp = 56 grams] and a maximum adult mass of 793 grams [Wwi = 793 grams] underscores the substantial scope for growth inherent in this species' ontogeny. These parameters collectively define a demographic profile well-suited to stable lacustrine environments.
